builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: IRTIQA: Evolving in English, Evaluated in Urdu -- Does Agent Self-Evolution Transfer from English to Urdu and Code-Switched Input?
summary: The paper does not replace an existing method; it introduces IRTIQA, an aligned English/Urdu/code-switched evaluation benchmark, and uses it to audit self-evolving agent frameworks (Tool-R0, AgentEvolver, Autogenesis) against their unevolved backbones. Adopting its implication means treating language parity as an explicit evaluation target, which costs building or reusing aligned multilingual test sets and, if self-evolution is pursued, RL-style training that exceeds a single 24 GB GPU budget for larger backbones. What can fail is assuming self-improvement generalizes across languages: RL-based evolution can widen the gap, hurting Urdu reasoning more than English, and code-switched inputs behave as a distinct failure condition rather than degraded translation.
rationale: The paper is a benchmark and a cautionary negative result rather than a deployable technique: it shows that self-evolution frameworks do not transfer gains equitably to low-resource languages, which is decision-relevant only if the reader serves non-English or code-switched users.

claims.statement: The paper does not replace an existing method; it introduces IRTIQA, an aligned English/Urdu/code-switched evaluation benchmark, and uses it to audit self-evolving agent frameworks (Tool-R0, AgentEvolver, Autogenesis) against their unevolved backbones. Adopting its implication means treating language parity as an explicit evaluation target, which costs building or reusing aligned multilingual test sets and, if self-evolution is pursued, RL-style training that exceeds a single 24 GB GPU budget for larger backbones. What can fail is assuming self-improvement generalizes across languages: RL-based evolution can widen the gap, hurting Urdu reasoning more than English, and code-switched inputs behave as a distinct failure condition rather than degraded translation.

AgentEvolver raises AppWorld goal completion from near zero to 20-36% across English, Urdu, and code-switched conditions, and Autogenesis improves SkillsBench pass rate from 16.48% to 22.22%; however, evolved systems remain stronger in English by up to 0.26 DROP F1, and RL-based evolution can degrade Urdu reasoning more than English.
